titulo: Square desktop robot: print, shop from the list, and assemble — robos-impressos
meta: A 20 cm desktop robot with a screen for a face: STL and 3MF files ready in the print orientation, a shopping list with estimated prices and links, and step-by-step assembly.
hero_h1: You print, shop from the list, and assemble your desktop robot
hero_lead: Robot projects often get stuck halfway: a screw is missing, a part doesn't fit in the printer, or nobody tells you what to buy. Here, the files are already laid out in the print orientation, the shopping list includes quantities, estimated prices, and links, and assembly takes you from the first threaded insert to the battery door.
hero_alt: Render of the square desktop robot: a white cube head with a dark panel and a screen showing two eyes, on top of a low gray base
hero_cap: Render of the actual model, the same one used to generate the print files. The screen shows the face the robot will display.
resumo: The square robot is a [[N_ALTURA]] cm desktop robot you can print at home and assemble. Its head is a cube with a 3.5-inch screen for a face; it rotates almost a full turn and tilts up and down. Inside are a Raspberry Pi, an Arduino, two servos, and a battery that charges via USB-C. You need a 3D printer with a 256 mm build plate, the parts on the shopping list, and a soldering iron. This is phase 1: the body and fittings. Programming (voice, camera, AI) comes in phase 2.
vistas_alt: Four views of the robot: front, three-quarter views from both sides, and back
resumo_nota: All images on this page are renders of the actual 3D model. Nothing has been printed yet: you will be the first to print it, starting with the test piece. The project's other robots are at
robo_h2: What will sit on your desk
robo_sub: A cube with a face on top of a low base. No screws are visible from the front: everything is secured from below or behind.
exp_alt: Exploded view: head cup, yellow frame with the Raspberry Pi and screen, face panel, fork, neck with gears, cover, and base with the boards
robo1_p: The screen, Raspberry Pi, and tilt servo are inside the head. The Arduino, battery, power converters, and neck rotation servo are inside the base. The cables run up through the hollow neck.
esq_alt: The PETG parts only: base, cover, neck, gears, fork, and head frame
robo2_p: The load-bearing parts are made of PETG: the base, cover, neck, gears, fork, and head frame. The white cup and dark face panel are made of PLA and simply fit over the robot.
mov1_p: A standard 180° servo moves two printed gears with 44 and 22 teeth. The neck rotates twice as far as the servo: almost a full turn.
mov2_p: The tilt servo is hidden inside the head. From the outside, you only see the slim neck.
mov3_p: The 3.5-inch screen plugs directly into the Raspberry Pi. The program draws the eyes and mouth on it; that’s phase 2.
robo_nota: The project checker tests the balance with the head in 10 positions. The result is at the end of this page.

cam_h2: From file to robot in 4 steps
cam_sub: The order matters: the first print takes less than an hour and helps you avoid losing a whole day of printer time.
cam1_p: A small coupon with the servo opening and insert and screw holes at three clearances. You’ll find out which clearance works with your printer before using up filament.
cam2_p: The files already have the parts laid flat and sorted by color. It takes about [[N_HORAS]] hours and [[N_GRAMAS]] g of filament, with no supports on any part.
cam3_p: Install [[N_INSERTOS]] brass inserts with a soldering iron, then assemble the base, the head on the workbench, and finally the head onto the base.
cam4_p: Battery, protection board, 5 V converter for the Raspberry Pi, and 6 V converter for the servos. The robot charges via USB-C without being opened.
cam_nota: Each step is explained in detail in the technical section just below.
tec_sub: You don’t need this section to understand the robot. It’s the manual: files, print settings, screws, steps, power, and proof that the parts fit together.
bx_sub: Everything is already positioned for printing, with the supported face against the build plate. You don’t need to rotate anything in the slicer.
bx1_p: A zip file with the [[N_DISTINTAS]] STL files, the [[N_MESAS]] 3MF build plate files, and the print instructions.
bx2_p: Each 3MF contains the parts of one color, already arranged on a 256 mm build plate. Open it in Bambu Studio and choose the filament.
bx2_link: open the build plate folder on GitHub
bx3_p: One file per part, for any slicer. The direct links are in the parts table below.
bx3_link: open the STL folder on GitHub
bx_nota: The 3MF files are generic: they contain only the geometry and position, with no print profile or color. They were checked again with a script, but haven’t been opened in Bambu Studio yet. If one won’t open, use the STL files.
imp_sub: Bambu Lab A1, 0.4 mm nozzle, 0.2 mm layer. PETG for load-bearing parts, PLA for parts that only cover something.
imp1_p: It is on build plate 06, together with the 4 Raspberry Pi spacers. Test the servo in the window, one insert in each of the 3 holes (3.9, 4.0 and 4.1 mm), and the M3, M2.5 and M2 screws. The dimple marks the size used by the design. If another clearance works better, change the value in cad/parametros.py (the FOLGA block) and generate the parts again.
teste_alt: Drawing of the test piece with the servo window and the insert and screw holes
imp1_mini: Click the image to enlarge. Nothing in this project has been printed yet, so this test comes first.
imp2_t: Print the build plates in this order
imp2_p: Start with the small parts that fit together, and print the two long pieces last. Each row has a direct link to the file.
mesas_alt: The build plates viewed from above, with the parts arranged by color
imp2_mini: The colors are suggestions. Changing the color makes no difference; changing PETG to PLA for load-bearing parts does.
imp3_p: The number of walls (perimeters) and the infill vary from part to part: gears and the fork need more. No part needs supports in the orientation provided in the file.
imp4_p: How much of each color, across all parts.
imp4_mini: Weight and time are volume-based estimates. The slicer will give you the actual figures.
reforcos_p: So you know what must not be made thinner if you modify the model.
mon_sub: The order below is the same one the checker tested: each part fits in from the indicated side without hitting anything already assembled.
mon_paraf_t: Screws and inserts, one by one
mon_paraf_p: There are [[N_INSERTOS]] M3 heat-set inserts. Seat them all before you start, using the soldering iron, slowly, until they are flush with the part's surface.
mon_passos_p: Steps marked (workbench) are done outside the robot, with the part in your hand.
mon_abrir_p: Replacing the battery or working on the boards does not require disassembling the head.
en_sub: Two 18650 batteries in series provide 6 to 8.4 V. From there, two separate lines branch off: one for the brain, the other for the motors.
en_f3: LM2596: 5 V for the Raspberry Pi · UBEC: 6 V for the 2 servos
en1_p: The LM2596 converter maintains 5 V until the battery drops to about 6.5 V. Set the output to 5.1 V with a multimeter before connecting the Pi. It delivers up to 3 A: use the Pi 4, or the Pi 5 without power-hungry USB accessories.
en2_p: The UBEC delivers 3 A continuously for the two MG996R servos. A 1000 µF capacitor on the output handles the startup surge. The program must not let both servos push against their end stops at the same time.
en3_p: The balance charger sits with its port in a window behind the base. It needs a third wire, soldered to the point joining the two cells. The protection board disconnects the battery before it is deeply discharged.
en_nota: What exists today is the location for each module and the decision about which ones to use. The wire-by-wire diagram and electrical test will come after the first assembly. Check the polarity with a multimeter before connecting any board: a shorted lithium battery can catch fire.
f2_h2: What already has a place for Phase 2
f2_sub: You don’t need to buy any of this now. The space, holes, and cable routing are already built into the parts.
f2_nota: Phase 2 (voice, camera, sensors, AI) hasn’t been built yet.
ver_h2: Proof that it fits, and what still needs to be proven
ver_sub: Actual output from the project verifier for this robot: [[N_TESTES]] tests run on the computer on the same parts you download.
ver_ok_li:
• Each STL is a closed mesh and fits on the 256 mm build plate.
  • No part passes through another part or component in 10 head positions.
  • Each part goes in and comes out through the side indicated in the assembly instructions.
  • The robot doesn’t tip over with the head at either extreme.
  • No part needs supports in the file’s print position.
ver_nao_t: What only printing can tell you
ver_nao_li:
• The actual clearances on your printer: that’s why the test part comes first.
  • The dimensions marked NC on purchased components.
  • The actual time and weight: these numbers are estimates made without a slicer.
  • The strength of the gears and fork in use.
  • The electrical side: no wires have been connected yet.
ver_nota: To generate the files and repeat the tests on your computer:
